optical-sensing-001.question: In a ToF LiDAR, SPADs (single-photon avalanche diodes) are used as receivers, and the photon arrival times for many pulses are recorded to build a histogram (time-correlated single-photon counting, TCSPC). What is the main advantage of this method?
choices: A SPAD measures the Doppler shift of the returning light photon by photon, so the object's velocity is obtained along with the range in a single measurement
Averaging round-trip times in a histogram determines the distance to an object at any range unambiguously, regardless of the pulse repetition rate
Even with only a few photons per pulse, reflected photons pile up at one arrival time, standing out from background light and dark counts arriving at random
optical-sensing-001.explanation: From distant or low-reflectivity objects, only a few photons or fewer return per pulse. A SPAD can detect even a single photon, but it also counts background light such as sunlight and dark counts at random times. Building a histogram of arrival times over many pulses makes photons from the reflection pile up at the position of the round-trip time, so they can be distinguished from the nearly uniform background. What a SPAD measures is the arrival time; it cannot measure a frequency shift of the light, so it cannot find velocity directly. Also, if the light does not return before the next pulse is sent, the distance becomes ambiguous, and the maximum unambiguous range is c/(2f_rep), limited to 150 m at a 1 MHz repetition rate. Under strong background light, counting bias due to SPAD dead time (pile-up) also needs attention.

optical-sensing-002.question: An FMCW LiDAR sweeps the optical frequency linearly over a bandwidth B = 1 GHz. Which value is closest to the range resolution ΔR = c/(2B)? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 15 cm
About 30 cm
About 7.5 cm
optical-sensing-002.explanation: ΔR = c/(2B) = 3.0×10⁸/(2 × 1×10⁹) = 0.15 m, or about 15 cm. With a sweep time T, the beat frequency from an object at range R is (B/T)(2R/c), and the frequency difference resolvable in a measurement time T is about 1/T, so the resolvable range difference is c/(2B), independent of the sweep time. About 30 cm drops the factor 2 for the round trip, giving c/B, and about 7.5 cm divides by 2 once too often. A resolution of 1.5 cm requires a 10 GHz sweep, and the linearity of the frequency sweep also affects the resolution. The measurable range is further limited by the coherence length (linewidth) of the laser, so FMCW systems use narrow-linewidth lasers.

optical-sensing-003.question: An FMCW LiDAR that ramps the optical frequency up and down in a triangle wave (up-chirp and down-chirp) measures an approaching object. Which method correctly obtains range and velocity from the beat frequencies f_up and f_down measured during the up and down ramps?
choices: The beat frequency corresponding to range comes from the difference of f_up and f_down, and the Doppler shift from their sum, respectively
The beat frequency corresponding to range comes from the average of f_up and f_down, and the Doppler shift from half their difference
Either beat frequency alone determines both range and velocity; the other is used only for confirmation
optical-sensing-003.explanation: Let f_R be the frequency difference due to range and f_D the Doppler shift. For an approaching object the returning light is shifted up in frequency, so the up-chirp beat is f_up = f_R − f_D and the down-chirp beat is f_down = f_R + f_D. Hence f_R = (f_up + f_down)/2 and f_D = (f_down − f_up)/2, and the velocity follows from f_D as v = f_D λ/2. For 1550 nm light, 1 m/s gives f_D ≈ 1.29 MHz. The option swapping difference and sum confuses this relation. A single beat gives only the sum or the difference of f_R and f_D, which cannot separate the two unknowns. Which beat is larger also tells whether the object is approaching or receding.

optical-sensing-004.question: A fiber Bragg grating (FBG) is written into the core of a single-mode fiber with an effective index of 1.447 as a periodic index structure with period Λ = 535.6 nm. Which value is closest to the strongly reflected wavelength (the Bragg wavelength λB = 2 n_eff Λ)?
choices: About 1550 nm
About 775 nm
About 1071 nm
optical-sensing-004.explanation: λB = 2 n_eff Λ = 2 × 1.447 × 535.6 nm ≈ 1550 nm. The weak reflections from each plane of the periodic structure all add in phase at the wavelength for which the round-trip path difference 2n_effΛ is exactly one wavelength, so only that wavelength is strongly reflected. About 775 nm drops the round-trip factor 2, and about 1071 nm uses 2Λ without multiplying by the effective index. The reflection bandwidth is usually narrow, about 0.1–1 nm, and other wavelengths are transmitted almost unchanged. This allows wavelength-multiplexed sensors in which many FBGs with different Bragg wavelengths are placed on a single fiber and read out by distinguishing their reflection wavelengths. FBGs are written by periodically changing the core index with ultraviolet interference fringes or a phase mask.

optical-sensing-005.question: A tensile strain of 500 µε (strain 5×10⁻⁴) is applied along the fiber axis to an FBG with a Bragg wavelength of 1550 nm. With the temperature constant and the shift of the Bragg wavelength given by ΔλB = (1 − pe) ε λB (effective photoelastic coefficient pe = 0.22), which value is closest to the wavelength shift?
choices: About 0.78 nm
About 0.17 nm
About 0.60 nm
optical-sensing-005.explanation: ΔλB = (1 − 0.22) × 5×10⁻⁴ × 1550 nm ≈ 0.60 nm. That is about 1.2 pm per µε, the typical strain sensitivity of an FBG in the 1550 nm band. Stretching the fiber lengthens the period Λ, but the photoelastic effect slightly lowers the effective index, so the wavelength increases by a factor (1 − pe) less. About 0.78 nm ignores the photoelastic effect, giving ελB, and about 0.17 nm multiplies by pe alone. If the reflection wavelength can be read with 1 pm resolution, strains of about 1 µε can be detected. Because a wavelength is not affected by fluctuations in light intensity or connection losses, FBGs measure stably even over long connected spans.

optical-sensing-006.question: When an FBG is used as a strain sensor, which combination of the reason temperature changes must be considered and the countermeasure is correct?
choices: The Bragg wavelength does not change with temperature, so no countermeasure is needed and every wavelength change can be attributed to strain (about 1.2 pm/µε)
The Bragg wavelength also shifts by about 10 pm/K (1550 nm band) with temperature, indistinguishable from strain, so a strain-free reference FBG is used to subtract the temperature part
A temperature rise only lowers the FBG's reflectance without shifting the Bragg wavelength, so the temperature part is corrected using the reflected intensity as a reference
optical-sensing-006.explanation: Because of the temperature dependence of the silica index (the thermo-optic effect) and thermal expansion, the Bragg wavelength changes by about 10 pm/K in the 1550 nm band. The strain sensitivity is about 1.2 pm/µε, so a 1 K temperature change gives a wavelength change as large as about 8 µε of strain, and the two cannot be distinguished from the wavelength alone. So a reference FBG, mounted at the same temperature but fixed so that no strain reaches it, is placed nearby and its wavelength change is subtracted. The option saying the wavelength does not change with temperature is wrong; in fact, this property makes the FBG usable as a temperature sensor. What mainly changes with temperature is the wavelength, not the reflectance, so correcting by intensity is also wrong. When bonded to a structure, strain from the thermal expansion of the host material is added as well.

optical-sensing-007.question: Which statement correctly describes how a Raman-scattering distributed temperature sensor (DTS) finds the temperature at each position along the fiber?
choices: It uses the fact that the frequency shift of the backscattered light (about 11 GHz in the 1550 nm band) changes with temperature, and measures that frequency at each position

From the backscatter of a light pulse, it finds, for each position set by the round-trip time, the intensity ratio of the strongly temperature-dependent anti-Stokes light to the weakly dependent Stokes light
It reads the reflection wavelengths of FBGs written at each position along the fiber by wavelength multiplexing
optical-sensing-007.explanation: Raman scattering in silica appears about 13 THz away from the incident light, and the intensity of the anti-Stokes light on the short-wavelength side depends strongly on temperature through the Boltzmann factor, which gives the number of molecules in excited vibrational states. The Stokes light on the long-wavelength side depends only weakly on temperature, so taking the ratio of the two cancels fluctuations in source power and fiber loss and yields the temperature. As with an OTDR, the position is found from the time between sending a pulse and the return of the scattered light. Using a frequency shift of about 11 GHz is the Brillouin method. Lining up FBGs is a quasi-distributed method that measures only the points with FBGs, unlike distributed sensing that measures every position along the fiber continuously. DTS is used to monitor the temperature of power cables, pipelines and wells.

optical-sensing-008.question: Which statement correctly describes distributed fiber sensors that use Brillouin scattering (BOTDR and BOTDA)?
choices: Because they use only the intensity ratio of the scattered light, they have no strain sensitivity and measure only the temperature at each position

It is elastic scattering from tiny fluctuations in the fiber's refractive index with no frequency change, so they find strain from the phase change of scattered light at the incident frequency, position by position

The frequency shift of the scattered light (about 10.8 GHz in the 1550 nm band) varies with both strain and temperature, so strain distributions can be measured, but the temperature part must be separated
optical-sensing-008.explanation: Brillouin scattering is scattering by sound waves (acoustic phonons) in the fiber, with a frequency shift νB = 2nVa/λ. For n = 1.45, a sound velocity Va = 5800 m/s and λ = 1.55 µm it is about 10.8 GHz. Because the sound velocity and index change with strain and temperature, νB changes by about 0.05 MHz/µε with strain and about 1 MHz/K with temperature, allowing strain distributions in structures to be measured over tens of km. Since it is sensitive to both, however, the Raman method or strain-free fibers are used alongside to separate the temperature contribution. Using only intensity and measuring only temperature is a mistaken description closer to the Raman method. Elastic scattering at the same frequency as the incident light is Rayleigh scattering. BOTDA uses stimulated Brillouin scattering between counter-propagating pump and probe light to obtain a strong signal.

optical-sensing-009.question: Which statement correctly describes the principle of distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), which uses a telecom fiber over tens of km as a vibration and sound sensor?
choices: Narrow-linewidth pulses are launched, and the time variation of the phase (interfered intensity) of the Rayleigh backscatter is tracked at each position
The signals of electrical microphones attached at regular intervals along the fiber are converted to light, multiplexed and transmitted over the fiber
It uses the change in the intensity of the Raman anti-Stokes light caused by vibration-induced strain, locating it by the round-trip time
optical-sensing-009.explanation: When narrow-linewidth laser pulses are launched, the Rayleigh backscatter from the many scattering points within the pulse length interferes, producing a trace whose intensity varies with position (φ-OTDR). When vibration or sound slightly stretches or compresses the fiber, the optical path length at that spot changes and so does the phase of the scattered light; by launching pulses repeatedly and tracking the phase change at each position, the whole fiber acts like an array of microphones. No electrical microphones are used; the fiber itself is the sensor. The intensity of Raman scattering changes with temperature but hardly responds to vibration. Each pulse is sent only after the previous scattered light has returned, so for a 50 km length (group index 1.468) the repetition rate is limited to about 2.0 kHz or less, and the measurable vibration frequency to half that.

optical-sensing-010.question: In an OCT system using a source with a Gaussian spectrum, a center wavelength of 840 nm and a spectral width (FWHM) of 50 nm, which value is closest to the axial resolution inside biological tissue with a refractive index of 1.35? Find it by dividing the resolution in air, Δz = (2 ln2/π) λ²/Δλ, by the tissue index.
choices: About 4.6 µm
About 6.2 µm
About 8.4 µm
optical-sensing-010.explanation: The resolution in air is Δz = 0.441 × (840 nm)²/50 nm ≈ 6.2 µm, and since the optical path length in tissue is n times longer, the physical depth resolution is 6.2/1.35 ≈ 4.6 µm. About 6.2 µm is the value in air, forgetting to divide by the index, and about 8.4 µm multiplies by the index instead of dividing. The axial resolution is set by the coherence length of the source and scales as λ²/Δλ, so a shorter center wavelength and a wider bandwidth give finer resolution. The 840 nm band has low water absorption and is used for imaging the retina of the eye. For strongly scattering tissue such as skin, the 1310 nm band is chosen because it reaches deeper, even at the cost of resolution. The lateral resolution is set separately from the axial one, by the focusing of the objective lens.

optical-sensing-011.question: In Fourier-domain (spectral-domain) OCT, which method correctly obtains depth information without moving the reference mirror?
choices: The interference strength between reference and signal light is measured with a single detector, and depth is set from its size, assuming that deeper reflections are always weaker
When a spectrometer resolves the interfering light by wavelength, deeper reflectors give finer fringes in the spectrum, so a Fourier transform over wavenumber is taken
The round-trip time of a light pulse is measured directly, finding the depth of each reflector as half the product of light speed and time, the same way as a ToF LiDAR does
optical-sensing-011.explanation: Light from a reflecting surface with a path difference of 2z relative to the reference produces fringes cos(2kz) (k is the wavenumber) on the spectrum, finer for deeper surfaces. Fourier transforming the spectrum with respect to wavenumber gives the reflection strength at all depths (the A-scan) at once. It is faster and more sensitive than time-domain OCT, which scans the reference mirror, and is the mainstream today. The maximum measurable depth is limited to about λ²/(4δλ), set by the spectrometer's wavelength resolution δλ. Measuring only the strength of the interference with one detector cannot separate reflection strength from depth. Resolving 10 µm in depth by ToF would require a time resolution of about 67 fs, which cannot be measured electronically, so OCT measures path difference by interference.

optical-sensing-012.question: An optical rotary encoder with 2500 slits per revolution counts every rising and falling edge of its A- and B-phase signals, which differ in phase by 90° (×4 decoding). Which value is closest to the rotation angle per count?
choices: About 0.144°
About 0.072°
About 0.036°
optical-sensing-012.explanation: ×4 decoding divides each period into four counts, so one revolution gives 2500 × 4 = 10000 counts, and one count is 360°/10000 = 0.036°. About 0.144° is 360°/2500, counting only the periods of the A phase without decoding, and about 0.072° is ×2 decoding, counting only the rising and falling edges of the A phase. Because the A and B phases are offset by a quarter period, the two signals have four transitions per period, and which changes first also reveals the direction of rotation. For finer measurement, interpolation is used, finding the phase by arctangent from sinusoidal A- and B-phase signals and dividing one period into hundreds to thousands of parts. To know the position at power-up, an index (Z-phase) signal or an absolute encoder is used.

optical-sensing-013.question: What is the main reason an optical incremental encoder outputs its two signals, the A and B phases, offset from each other by a quarter period (90°)?
choices: For redundancy, so that if one signal fails, the other can take over the counting without interruption
Adding the two signals together cancels fluctuations in the light-source brightness and slow temperature drift
Which signal changes first shows the direction of motion, and each period can be split into four for counting
optical-sensing-013.explanation: With only one signal, the number of light–dark cycles gives the amount of movement, but not which way it moved. Offsetting the A and B phases by a quarter period makes A change before B in the forward direction and B before A in reverse, so the direction can be determined. The rising and falling edges of the two signals give four transitions per period, providing ×4 resolution. For redundancy, two in-phase signals would suffice, with no need for a 90° offset. Fluctuations in source brightness are cancelled by receiving the A phase and its inverted signal differentially, but that is not the purpose of the phase difference between A and B. Signals offset by 90° correspond to sin and cos, so the phase can also be found by arctangent to finely interpolate within a period.

optical-sensing-014.question: A differential laser Doppler velocimeter (LDV) crosses two 532 nm laser beams at a crossing angle (full angle between the beams) of 10°. Taking the fringe spacing in the crossing region as d = λ/(2 sin(θ/2)), which value is closest to the frequency at which the scattered light intensity fluctuates (the Doppler frequency f = v/d) for a particle crossing at 2 m/s perpendicular to the fringes?
choices: About 655 kHz
About 7.5 MHz
About 1.31 MHz
optical-sensing-014.explanation: The fringe spacing is d = 532 nm/(2 sin5°) = 532 nm/0.1743 ≈ 3.05 µm, and the scattered light goes through one light–dark cycle each time the particle crosses a fringe, so f = v/d = 2/(3.05×10⁻⁶) ≈ 655 kHz. About 7.5 MHz uses the formula 2v/λ for a single beam reflected straight back, which is not the differential arrangement. About 1.31 MHz uses sinθ instead of sin(θ/2), halving the fringe spacing. In the differential arrangement the frequency depends only on the crossing angle and wavelength, not on the direction from which the scattered light is observed, so the receiving optics can be placed freely. Only the velocity component perpendicular to the fringes is measured, and in flow measurements small particles (tracers) are added to the flow to obtain scattered light.

optical-sensing-015.question: In a differential laser Doppler velocimeter (LDV), the frequency of one of the two beams is sometimes shifted by 40 MHz with an acousto-optic device (Bragg cell). What is the main purpose?
choices: To raise the scattered-light intensity and the SNR, so that even small-diameter particles can be detected without being buried in noise, widening the range of measurable particles
The fringes then move at a constant speed, so even a stationary particle gives a 40 MHz signal, and whether it is above or below 40 MHz gives the direction of the velocity
To change the wavelength of one beam with the Bragg cell, effectively widening the crossing angle so that the fringe spacing becomes finer and the velocity resolution improves
optical-sensing-015.explanation: Without a frequency shift, the signal frequency is f = |v|/d, the same whichever way the particle moves, and a particle with nearly zero velocity gives no signal. Giving the two beams a 40 MHz difference makes the fringes in the crossing region move at a constant speed, so even a stationary particle produces a 40 MHz signal. With a fringe spacing of 3.05 µm, a particle at 2 m/s gives about 40.66 MHz or about 39.34 MHz depending on its direction, and whether the frequency is above or below 40 MHz reveals the direction. Shifting the frequency by 40 MHz changes the light's wavelength only negligibly, so the fringe spacing and the scattered intensity hardly change. Laser vibrometers that measure surface vibration likewise determine direction with heterodyne detection using such a frequency shift.

optical-sensing-016.question: In spectral-domain OCT, the interference spectrum centered at 840 nm is sampled with a wavelength interval of 0.05 nm per pixel of the spectrometer's image sensor. Taking the maximum imaging depth (the range on one side of zero path difference) as z_max = λ₀²/(4δλ), where δλ is the wavelength interval per pixel, which value is closest to the depth in air?
choices: About 7.1 mm
About 14 mm
About 3.5 mm
optical-sensing-016.explanation: A reflector at depth z produces fringes in the spectrum with period π/z in wavenumber k = 2π/λ, finer for deeper reflectors. Requiring at least two samples per fringe period at the per-pixel wavenumber spacing gives z_max = λ₀²/(4δλ). Substituting, (840 nm)²/(4 × 0.05 nm) = 7.06×10⁵ nm²/0.2 nm ≈ 3.5×10⁶ nm, about 3.5 mm. About 7.1 mm divides by 2 instead of 4, and about 14 mm is λ₀²/δλ; neither applies the sampling condition correctly. In tissue the depth is divided by the refractive index, and deeper reflectors lose sensitivity because their fringes are washed out by the pixel size and spectrometer resolution.

optical-sensing-017.question: The Bragg wavelength of an FBG in the 1550 nm band increases by about 10 pm per kelvin. Which is the main cause of this temperature dependence? The linear expansion coefficient of silica fiber is about 0.55×10⁻⁶ /K.
choices: Mainly the thermo-optic effect, by which the refractive index of silica increases with temperature; lengthening of the grating period by thermal expansion contributes only about a tenth of that

Mainly lengthening of the grating period Λ by thermal expansion of the fiber; the refractive index does not depend on temperature, so the change has the same fractional size as the expansion coefficient
The core index decreases with temperature, shortening the wavelength, but the larger thermal expansion of the coating stretches the fiber, so overall the wavelength increases
optical-sensing-017.explanation: The fractional change of the Bragg wavelength λB = 2n_eff Λ is ΔλB/λB = (α + ξ)ΔT, where α is the linear expansion coefficient and ξ = (1/n)dn/dT is the thermo-optic coefficient. About 10 pm/K at 1550 nm is a fractional rate of about 6.5×10⁻⁶ /K, and the expansion coefficient of 0.55×10⁻⁶ /K is only about a tenth of that. The rest comes from the thermo-optic effect, the increase of the silica index with temperature. Thermal expansion alone would give about 0.85 pm/K, an order of magnitude smaller than observed. Saying that the silica index decreases with temperature has the sign backwards. Bonding the fiber to a material with large expansion changes the sensitivity, but for a bare fiber the main cause is the thermo-optic effect.

optical-sensing-018.question: In a Raman distributed temperature sensor, the ratio R of the anti-Stokes to Stokes intensities follows R ∝ exp(−hΔν/kT), where Δν = 13.2 THz is the Raman shift of silica and the wavelength-dependent prefactor is independent of temperature. Near 300 K, which value is closest to the fractional change of the ratio per kelvin, (1/R)(dR/dT)? Use h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s and k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K.
choices: About 0.33%/K
About 0.70%/K
About 0.11%/K
optical-sensing-018.explanation: Since ln R = −hΔν/(kT) + constant, (1/R)(dR/dT) = hΔν/(kT²). With hΔν/k = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ × 13.2×10¹² / 1.38×10⁻²³ ≈ 634 K, this is 634/300² ≈ 7.0×10⁻³, about 0.70%/K. About 0.33%/K is 1/T, which assumes the ratio is proportional to temperature. About 0.11%/K wrongly uses h/2π instead of h. Because a ratio is taken, fluctuations in source power and losses common to both signals cancel, and a 1 K change can be read as a change of about 0.7% in the ratio. The anti-Stokes signal is weak, however, so many pulses are averaged to improve accuracy.

optical-sensing-019.question: An absolute optical rotary encoder, which keeps its position even after power-off, reads the angle as a binary code from the light and dark pattern of several concentric tracks. Why is a Gray code, rather than ordinary binary, commonly used for this code?
choices: Codes for adjacent positions differ in only one bit, so even if the tracks are read at slightly different instants at a boundary, the error is at most one step
Each bit carries more information, so it achieves the same resolution with fewer tracks than ordinary binary, letting the disk be smaller and halving the number of photodetectors
The light-dark boundaries of all tracks line up at the same angles, so all tracks switch simultaneously and no error at all occurs even if the reading instants differ somewhat
optical-sensing-019.explanation: In ordinary binary, going from 7 (0111) to 8 (1000) changes four bits at once. If the track boundaries or the detector responses are slightly misaligned, there are moments when a completely different value such as 1111 or 0000 is read. In a Gray code adjacent codes always differ in exactly one bit, so a misread at any boundary gives at most the neighboring value. Representing 2ⁿ steps with n bits is the same as ordinary binary, so the number of tracks is not reduced. It is ordinary binary in which boundaries coincide and switch together, and that is what causes misreading. The Gray code that is read is converted to ordinary binary by a circuit.

optical-sensing-020.question: A triangulation displacement sensor shines a laser spot on the target and images it onto an image sensor with a lens (focal length f) placed a baseline b away from the source, finding the distance z from the image position. If the image position varies as x ≈ bf/z, which statement about the distance resolution, for a fixed error in reading the image position, is correct?
choices: The distance error is independent of z, so the near and far ends of the measuring range have the same resolution, and the baseline does not affect the resolution
The distance error is proportional to z², becoming about four times worse when the distance doubles, which is offset by lengthening the baseline or focal length
The distance error is proportional to z, doubling at twice the distance, and a shorter baseline makes the image move more and improves the resolution
optical-sensing-020.explanation: Differentiating x = bf/z gives dx/dz = −bf/z², so an error Δx in the image position gives a distance error Δz = z²Δx/(bf). Doubling the distance makes Δz four times larger for the same Δx. A larger baseline b or focal length f makes the image move more and improves resolution, but the instrument grows and nearby objects more easily fall out of the field of view. Choices claiming a constant error or one proportional to z overlook that x is inversely proportional to z. A shorter baseline makes the image move less and worsens the resolution. Because of this behavior, triangulation suits precise measurement at short distances, while ToF and other methods are used at long range.

optical-sensing-021.question: In OCT the axial (depth) resolution is set by the spectral width (coherence length) of the source, and the lateral resolution (along the scan direction) is set by the numerical aperture of the lens focusing onto the sample. To make the lateral resolution finer, the lens NA is doubled. Which change is correct? (For a focused Gaussian beam, take the depth of focus as proportional to the square of the spot size.)
choices: Both the lateral and the axial resolution improve to about 1/2, and the depth range that stays sharp is unchanged
The lateral resolution improves to about 1/2, but the depth of focus shrinks to about 1/4, narrowing the depth range that stays sharp
The lateral resolution improves to about 1/2, and the depth of focus also doubles, so deep regions stay sharp
optical-sensing-021.explanation: OCT separates depth by low-coherence interference, so the axial resolution is set by the coherence length and does not depend on the lens NA. The lateral resolution is the focal spot size, which halves when the NA is doubled. The depth of focus (twice the Rayleigh range), however, scales with the square of the spot size and shrinks to about 1/4, so the lateral image blurs away from focus. The option in which the axial resolution also improves overlooks that the two resolutions are set by different factors. The option with a deeper focus has the direction reversed. Retinal OCT therefore often uses a modest NA to keep a depth range of a few mm.

optical-sensing-022.question: A diffraction-interference linear encoder overlaps and interferes the +1st and −1st orders diffracted by a scale grating with a 4 µm period. When the scale moves by one period, the phases of the +1st and −1st orders change by +2π and −2π. Which combination of the displacement for one period of the interference signal and the resolution when that period is electrically subdivided (interpolated) by 1000 is correct?
choices: Signal period 4 µm, resolution 4 nm
Signal period 1 µm, resolution 1 nm
Signal period 2 µm, resolution 2 nm
optical-sensing-022.explanation: When the scale moves by Δx, the phases of the +1st and −1st orders change by ±2πΔx/p, so their phase difference changes by 4πΔx/p. The interference signal goes through one period each time the phase difference changes by 2π, so the signal period is p/2 = 2 µm. Subdividing it by 1000 gives a resolution of 2 µm/1000 = 2 nm. A 4 µm signal period counts the phase change of only one order. 1 µm double-counts the change in phase difference. Compared with counting the light and dark of a grating's shadow, this gives a finer signal period, so it is used for precise positioning.

optical-sensing-023.question: A fiber-optic gyroscope has a fiber of length L = 1000 m wound into a coil of diameter D = 0.10 m and measures the Earth's rotation (angular rate Ω = 7.3×10⁻⁵ rad/s). Taking the phase difference between the clockwise and counterclockwise light (Sagnac effect) as Δφ = 2πLDΩ/(λc) with λ = 1.55 µm and c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s, which value is closest to Δφ?
choices: About 1.0×10⁻⁴ rad
About 4.9×10⁻⁵ rad
About 1.6×10⁻⁵ rad
optical-sensing-023.explanation: Δφ = 2π × 1000 × 0.10 × 7.3×10⁻⁵ /(1.55×10⁻⁶ × 3.0×10⁸) = 4.59×10⁻²/465 ≈ 9.9×10⁻⁵ rad, about 1.0×10⁻⁴ rad. About 4.9×10⁻⁵ rad uses the radius instead of the diameter, and about 1.6×10⁻⁵ rad omits the factor 2π. The phase difference is proportional to the enclosed area times the number of turns, so winding a longer fiber raises the sensitivity, and it does not depend on the fiber's refractive index. Because both beams travel the same path in opposite directions, path changes from temperature and vibration nearly cancel, but measuring phases below 10⁻⁴ rad relies on phase modulation to extract the signal.

optical-sensing-024.question: A long-period fiber grating (LPG), with a period of several hundred µm, can sense the refractive index of a liquid around the fiber, unlike an FBG with a period just under 1 µm. Which is the correct reason?
choices: With a long period, the Bragg wavelength is set directly by the index of the surrounding medium, so measuring the wavelength of the reflected light gives the index directly
Because the period is long, it has no sensitivity to strain or temperature and its transmission responds only to the surrounding index, so no temperature correction is needed
It couples core light into co-propagating cladding modes whose effective index depends on the surrounding index, so the wavelength of the transmission loss dip shifts
optical-sensing-024.explanation: An FBG reflects by coupling the core light into the counter-propagating core mode. The core-mode light stays in and near the core and barely touches the surroundings, so it is insensitive to the outside index. An LPG, with its long period, couples core light into co-propagating cladding modes, which are soon lost, so a loss dip appears in transmission at particular wavelengths. Cladding modes reach into the outer medium, so their effective index, and the dip wavelength, change with the surrounding index. An LPG is also strongly sensitive to strain and temperature, so saying it responds only to index is wrong; temperature compensation is needed.

optical-sensing-025.question: Which statement correctly describes a flash LiDAR, which illuminates the whole field of view at once with a pulse and measures the round-trip time at every pixel of a 2D receiver array, compared with a LiDAR that scans a narrow beam?
choices: Spreading the light over the whole field is offset by collecting it with all pixels at once, so the return per pixel equals that of scanning and the maximum range does not change
It has no moving parts and measures all pixels at once, but spreading the light over the field weakens the return per pixel, making long range hard to reach
Because the scene is lit at once, each pixel finds distance from the size of the object's image and the object's dimensions rather than the round-trip time, so no per-pixel timing is needed
optical-sensing-025.explanation: A flash LiDAR has no moving mirrors and gets the distance at every pixel from a single shot, so it is robust to vibration and images are not distorted in fast scenes. In exchange, the source light is spread over the whole field, so the light reaching an object within one pixel's view is far weaker than when a narrow beam lights that direction. Source power is also capped by eye-safety rules, so distant or weakly reflecting objects are hard to measure, and flash LiDAR suits short range. The return strength is set by the illumination density, so collecting with all pixels does not raise the per-pixel signal. Distance comes from the round-trip time at each pixel, not from image size.

optical-sensing-026.question: Two gratings of period p = 20 µm are overlaid with their lines tilted by θ = 0.01 rad relative to each other, producing broad moiré fringes. Which value is closest to the moiré fringe spacing P ≈ p/θ?
choices: About 0.20 µm
About 2.0 mm
About 1.0 mm
optical-sensing-026.explanation: P ≈ p/θ = 20 µm/0.01 = 2000 µm, about 2.0 mm. The exact expression is P = p/(2 sin(θ/2)), which gives the same value for small θ. When one grating moves by one period p perpendicular to its lines, the moiré fringes move by one spacing P, so the motion appears magnified by 1/θ = 100. About 0.20 µm multiplies p by θ, and about 1.0 mm divides by 2θ. Optical encoders and displacement sensors read these moiré fringes with a few photodetectors, detecting the fine motion of the grating as a large change in brightness. The direction in which the fringes move also gives the direction of the grating's motion.

optical-sensing-027.question: An interrogator that covers a 40 nm wavelength range distinguishes FBGs along one fiber by their Bragg wavelengths. Each FBG experiences strains of ±1000 µε, and the strain sensitivity is 1.2 pm/µε. If each FBG is allotted its range of variation plus a 0.6 nm margin so that neighboring ranges do not overlap, what is the maximum number of FBGs that can be placed? (Ignore temperature changes.)
optical-sensing-027.explanation: At ±1000 µε the Bragg wavelength moves by ±1.2 nm, a span of 2.4 nm. Adding the 0.6 nm margin gives 3.0 nm per grating, and 40/3.0 ≈ 13.3, so up to 13 FBGs fit. 16 divides by 2.4 nm without the margin (16.7), and 22 overlooks the ± and takes the span as 1.2 nm (40/1.8 ≈ 22). In practice the wavelength also changes by about 10 pm/K with temperature, so room for the operating temperature range must be allotted too, and even fewer gratings fit. To place more, wavelength division is combined with telling identical-wavelength FBGs apart by the time their reflections take to return.

optical-sensing-028.question: Fiber-optic gyroscopes often use a broad-spectrum source such as a superluminescent diode (SLD) rather than a narrow-linewidth laser. Which is the main reason?
choices: The Sagnac phase difference is proportional to the source's spectral width, so broadband light gives a larger phase difference for the same rotation and higher sensitivity
A narrow-linewidth laser cannot give the clockwise and counterclockwise waves the same frequency, so a large phase difference appears even without rotation
With a short coherence length, parasitic light from backscattering and polarization leakage hardly interferes with the main light, which suppresses noise and drift
optical-sensing-028.explanation: Rayleigh backscattering and light leaking between polarization axes arise inside the fiber. With a laser of long coherence length, this parasitic light interferes with the main light and causes phase noise and drift, and the Kerr effect also produces errors through clockwise–counterclockwise asymmetry. A source like an SLD with a spectral width of tens of nanometers has a coherence length of only tens of micrometers, so parasitic light with a different path length barely interferes with the main light. The Sagnac phase difference 2πLDΩ/(λc) depends on the center wavelength and is not proportional to the spectral width. The clockwise and counterclockwise waves are split from the same source, so their frequencies are the same from the start.

optical-sensing-029.question: In fringe projection, a sinusoidal fringe pattern is projected obliquely onto an object and photographed by a camera from another direction to measure the object's 3D shape. Which statement correctly gives the principle used to obtain height?
choices: It uses the triangulation relation by which fringes shift sideways with object height, finds the fringe phase at each pixel by phase shifting, and joins the 2π jumps before converting to height
The fringe spacing changes in proportion to the distance to the object, so measuring the spacing at each pixel gives the height directly without finding any phase
Fringe brightness depends only on the surface reflectance, so the reflectance is found from the brightness distribution and differences in reflectance are converted into height differences
optical-sensing-029.explanation: Because the projection and viewing directions are at an angle, the projected fringes appear shifted sideways at points of different height. This is the same relation as point-by-point triangulation, and the shift appears as a change in fringe phase. With phase shifting, in which several images are taken with the fringe phase stepped by π/2, the phase can be found at each pixel while removing the effects of uneven reflectance and background light. The phase wraps every 2π, so it is unwrapped before being converted to height. The fringe spacing also changes slightly with distance, but the height information lies mainly in the shift of fringe position. Brightness depends on both reflectance and illumination, so it carries no height information. Since all pixels are measured at once, the shape is obtained faster than by scanning a point or a line.

optical-sensing-030.question: A fiber-optic current sensor winds an optical fiber N times around a current-carrying conductor and measures the current from the rotation of the plane of linearly polarized light traveling in the fiber. Which statement correctly describes its principle and features?
choices: Heating by the current changes the fiber's refractive index and rotates the polarization plane, so the conductor temperature is found from the rotation and converted into current
The magnetic field of the current rotates the polarization plane, but the rotation depends on the distance from the conductor to the fiber, so the conductor must be held precisely in place
It uses Faraday rotation; the total rotation around a closed loop is proportional to the enclosed current and the number of turns, whatever the conductor's position
optical-sensing-030.explanation: In the Faraday effect, the rotation angle of the polarization plane is proportional to the integral of the magnetic-field component along the propagation direction over the path, with the Verdet constant V as the coefficient. If the fiber forms closed loops around the conductor, Ampère's law makes the line integral of the field equal to the enclosed current, so the rotation is fixed by the number of turns and the current alone, as Vμ₀NI. The conductor may sit anywhere inside the loop, and the effects of outside currents cancel. The sensor does not rely on index changes from heating. Because it is electrically insulating and immune to electromagnetic noise, it is used to measure current in high-voltage power equipment. Birefringence induced by bending disturbs the rotation, so the fiber type and winding need care.

optical-sensing-031.question: An optical linear encoder with a 20 µm scale period moves at 0.5 m/s. Which combination correctly gives the frequency of the A-phase signal and the number of counts per second when every rising and falling edge of the A and B phases is counted (×4 decoding)?
choices: A phase about 100 kHz; about 400,000 counts per second
A phase about 25 kHz; about 100,000 counts per second
A phase about 25 kHz; about 25,000 counts per second
optical-sensing-031.explanation: Each time the scale moves one period, the A-phase signal goes through one cycle, so its frequency is v/p = 0.5/(20×10⁻⁶) = 2.5×10⁴ Hz, about 25 kHz. ×4 decoding counts each cycle four times, giving about 100,000 counts per second, with one count corresponding to 5 µm. About 25,000 counts per second forgets the ×4 factor. About 100 kHz wrongly applies the factor of 4 to the signal frequency as well; decoding only counts the signal more finely and does not change its frequency. Because the receiver, interpolation circuits, and counter can only follow up to some frequency, finer interpolation lowers the maximum measurable speed. Fast machines choose the interpolation factor by balancing resolution against maximum speed.

optical-sensing-032.question: Swept-source OCT (SS-OCT) sweeps the source wavelength in time, records the interference intensity with a single photodetector as a function of time, and Fourier-transforms it with respect to wavenumber. Which combination correctly gives what mainly sets the axial resolution and the measurable depth range?
choices: The resolution is set by the width of the swept wavelength range, and the depth range by the instantaneous linewidth at each moment and the fineness of sampling
The resolution is set by the instantaneous linewidth at each moment, and the depth range becomes deeper as the swept wavelength range gets wider
The resolution is set only by the speed of the photodetector and A/D converter, and the depth range becomes deeper with more sweeps per second
optical-sensing-032.explanation: As in spectral-domain OCT, the axial resolution is set by the spectral width of the source; in SS-OCT, the wider the swept wavelength range, the finer the resolution (Δz ∝ λ²/Δλ). Deeper reflectors produce finer fringes in wavenumber, so a broad instantaneous linewidth washes them out and weakens the signal from deep layers. The depth range is therefore set by the coherence length given by the instantaneous linewidth and by how finely the wavenumber is sampled in one sweep. The combination that swaps how resolution and depth range are determined is wrong. The speed of the photodetector and A/D converter affects the depth range through sampling but does not set the resolution, and more sweeps per second raise the fringe frequency, so with the same detector the depth range actually becomes shallower.

optical-sensing-033.question: In an optical rotary encoder, if the center of the scale disk is slightly offset from the rotation axis (eccentricity), the angle reading has an error that repeats once per revolution. Which method reduces this error?
choices: Place the A- and B-phase read heads 90° apart on the disk and subtract the eccentricity found from the phase difference between the two signals
Dividing each period finely with ×4 decoding or interpolation reduces the eccentricity error in proportion to the division factor
Place a second read head 180° opposite across the disk and average the two readings
optical-sensing-033.explanation: With an eccentricity e, the scale at the read head is displaced along the circumference by about e sinθ, giving an angle error of about (e/r) sinθ, where r is the scale radius, that repeats once per revolution. At the position 180° opposite the displacement has the opposite sign, so averaging the two heads cancels this once-per-revolution error. Precision angle measurement goes further and places more heads at equal intervals to reduce higher-order errors. Decoding and interpolation only count each period more finely and do not reduce the displacement of the scale itself. The A and B phases are signals taken within one head, offset by a quarter of the scale period, to tell the direction of rotation.

optical-sensing-034.question: When a pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR measures the ground beyond a canopy of leaves, a single pulse can return several reflections (echoes) at different times. Which correctly explains this and how it is used?
choices: They are apparent reflections from pulses split by fluctuations in the refractive index of air, so only the averaged time is used and the other echoes are discarded
Leaves and ground both fall within the spreading beam and return from different distances, so the last echo gives the ground height
They are multiple reflections of light bouncing between the ground and the leaves, so using only the first echo removes the others as noise
optical-sensing-034.explanation: A LiDAR beam spreads gradually and can be tens of centimeters wide at a distance, so it may cover part of the foliage and the ground visible through gaps at the same time. Light reflected at each distance R returns after 2R/c, so one pulse gives several echoes at different times. The first echo often comes from the top of the canopy and the last from the ground, so recording both measures tree height and terrain at once; some systems record the full return waveform. Fluctuations in air do not split the pulse, and multiple reflections between leaves and ground are weak and not the main source of the echoes. Using only the first echo would lose the ground information.

optical-sensing-035.question: When a differential laser Doppler velocimeter (LDV) measures a gas flow, small tracer particles are seeded into the flow. Which describes correctly how the particle size is chosen?
choices: Larger particles scatter more light but lag behind rapid changes in the flow, so the size is a compromise between tracking ability and signal strength
Since the fringe motion rather than the particles is measured, bigger particles with stronger signals are always better and tracking does not matter
Making the particle diameter equal to the fringe spacing maximizes the modulation of scattered light, so the size is set by the fringe spacing alone
optical-sensing-035.explanation: An LDV measures the speed of particles crossing the interference fringes in the beam-crossing region. Unless the particles move with the flow, the flow velocity is not measured correctly. Larger, heavier particles lag behind changes in the flow because of inertia and follow fine turbulent fluctuations and sudden accelerations poorly. Smaller particles scatter less light and lower the signal S/N, so oil droplets about 1 µm in diameter are often used in gases. Without a frequency shift the fringes are stationary, and it is the particle motion that is measured. A particle comparable in size to the fringe spacing covers bright and dark fringes at once and actually weakens the modulation, so particles much smaller than the spacing are preferred, and matching the spacing is wrong.

optical-sensing-036.question: In a pulsed ToF LiDAR, the whole beam falls on a diffuse (Lambertian) surface of 10% reflectance at a distance of 100 m. Viewing the surface head-on, take the ratio of the power returned to the receiving lens (diameter 25 mm) to the transmitted power as P_r/P_t = ρA/(πR²), where ρ is the reflectance, A the lens area and R the distance. Which value is closest (atmospheric loss ignored)?
choices: About 4.9×10⁻⁹
About 3.9×10⁻¹⁰
About 1.6×10⁻⁹
optical-sensing-036.explanation: The lens area is A = π(0.0125 m)² ≈ 4.91×10⁻⁴ m², so P_r/P_t = 0.10 × 4.91×10⁻⁴/(π × 100²) ≈ 1.6×10⁻⁹. Light reflected by a Lambertian surface has its maximum intensity ρP_t/π along the normal, so the denominator is πR². About 4.9×10⁻⁹ forgets to divide by π. About 3.9×10⁻¹⁰ divides by 4πR² as if the reflected light spread uniformly in all directions, which mistreats the angular distribution of a diffuse surface. The returned light falls off as the inverse square of the distance, and even with 1 W of peak power the received light is only on the order of nW, so sensitive receivers such as APDs and SPADs are used for long range. If the beam is larger than the object, the return is weaker still.

optical-sensing-037.question: Light is directed from inside a prism onto its base, which is coated with a thin gold film (about 50 nm thick), under total internal reflection, and the reflectance is measured as a function of the angle of incidence; at a certain angle the reflectance drops sharply (a surface plasmon resonance sensor in the Kretschmann configuration). Which statement about this sensor is correct?
choices: Light is absorbed at the angle where the p-polarized evanescent wave couples to the gold surface plasmon, and the angle shifts with the sample index
It occurs equally for s and p polarization, and the angle of the dip is set only by the gold film thickness, independent of the sample index
The sample molecules are labeled with fluorescent dyes, and the amount bound to the gold is found from the fluorescence excited by the totally reflected light
optical-sensing-037.explanation: Under total internal reflection in the prism, an evanescent wave extends into the gold film. At the angle where its wavenumber along the interface, k₀n_p sinθ (n_p the prism index), matches that of the surface plasmon propagating along the gold–sample interface, light energy transfers to the collective oscillation of the free electrons in the gold and the reflectance drops sharply. Surface plasmons can be excited only by p-polarized light, which has an electric-field component normal to the interface; with s polarization the reflectance hardly dips. The plasmon wavenumber is set by the refractive index within a few hundred nm of the gold, so when molecules bind to antibodies or the like on the surface and raise the index slightly, the resonance angle shifts to larger values, allowing the amount and rate of binding to be measured without fluorescent labels.

optical-sensing-038.question: A ring laser gyroscope measures rotation from the frequency difference between two laser beams circulating clockwise and counterclockwise in a ring cavity, but below a certain rotation rate the frequency difference becomes zero and rotation can no longer be detected (lock-in). Which correctly combines the cause and the usual remedy?
choices: The Earth's rotation always offsets the two frequencies and cancels slower rotations, so the Earth's rate is added back by calculation
Backscattering at the mirrors couples the two beams and pulls their frequencies together, so a small mechanical oscillation (dither) of the body avoids the dead band
At slow rotation the two optical paths become equal and the fringes vanish, so the source is replaced with a broad-spectrum source to restore fringes
optical-sensing-038.explanation: In a ring laser, rotation shifts the resonance conditions of the clockwise and counterclockwise beams and produces a frequency difference proportional to the angular rate, Δf = 4AΩ/(λP), where A is the enclosed area and P the perimeter. However, when a little light backscattered at the mirror surfaces enters the counter-propagating beam, the two oscillations couple, and while the frequency difference is small they are pulled to the same frequency. Dither, which shakes the body with a small amplitude, is therefore used so that on average the gyro operates outside the dead band. The Earth's rotation is one of the rotations to be detected, not the cause of lock-in. Passive gyros such as the fiber-optic gyro, which interfere light from an external source, do not show this pulling, and broad-spectrum sources are used there to reduce interference from parasitic light.

optical-sensing-039.question: A chromatic confocal displacement sensor focuses white light with a lens that deliberately has large axial chromatic aberration, passes the light reflected from the sample through a pinhole and measures it with a spectrometer. Which correctly describes how the distance is obtained?
choices: It counts the period of the interference fringes in the reflected spectrum and finds the surface position from the relation between fringe period and the path difference between the front and back surfaces
It reads the lateral position of the spot on the sample surface with an image sensor and finds the distance by triangulation from the baseline and focal length
Each wavelength focuses at a different depth and only the one focused on the surface passes the pinhole, so the distance follows from that wavelength
optical-sensing-039.explanation: A lens with chromatic aberration focuses short wavelengths closer and long wavelengths farther away. Light of the wavelength focused on the sample surface returns sharply focused at the pinhole, while defocused wavelengths spread around the pinhole and are blocked. The measured spectrum therefore shows a single peak, and with the wavelength-to-distance relation calibrated in advance, the distance is obtained with sub-µm resolution and no moving parts. For a transparent film, the two peaks from the front and back surfaces also give its thickness. Finding the path difference from the period of spectral fringes is the method of white-light interferometry and OCT, and using the lateral position of the spot is the principle of triangulation displacement sensors.

optical-sensing-040.question: An optical fiber oxygen sensor uses a film containing a dye whose luminescence is quenched by oxygen (such as a ruthenium complex) and measures the luminescence lifetime τ. The lifetime follows the Stern–Volmer equation τ₀/τ = 1 + K_SV p, where τ₀ is the lifetime without oxygen and p the oxygen partial pressure, with τ₀ = 5.0 µs and K_SV = 0.050 kPa⁻¹. If the lifetime is measured as 2.5 µs, which value is closest to the oxygen partial pressure?
choices: About 20 kPa
About 40 kPa
About 10 kPa
optical-sensing-040.explanation: Since τ₀/τ = 5.0/2.5 = 2.0, K_SV p = 2.0 − 1 = 1.0 and p = 1.0/0.050 = 20 kPa, close to the oxygen partial pressure of air (about 21 kPa). About 40 kPa forgets to subtract 1 and takes 2.0/0.050, and about 10 kPa takes the fractional decrease of the lifetime, 1 − τ/τ₀ = 0.5, as K_SV p. Oxygen molecules colliding with excited dye molecules take up their energy and return them to the ground state without emission (dynamic quenching), so more oxygen means a shorter lifetime and weaker luminescence. Measuring the lifetime rather than the intensity makes the result insensitive to dye bleaching, source intensity and changes in fiber bending loss. At higher partial pressures the lifetime changes less for the same change in pressure, so the sensitivity is highest at low partial pressures.

optical-sensing-041.question: In a Raman distributed temperature sensor, pulses 10 ns wide are launched into the fiber. Assuming the time resolution of the backscattered light is set by the pulse width, and using the spatial resolution Δz = cτ/(2n_g) (τ is the pulse width, n_g = 1.47 is the group index of the fiber, c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s), which value is closest to Δz?
choices: About 2.0 m
About 1.5 m
About 1.0 m
optical-sensing-041.explanation: Δz = 3.0×10⁸ × 10×10⁻⁹ / (2 × 1.47) ≈ 1.02 m, about 1.0 m. Backscatter arriving at a given moment comes from within the fiber length cτ/n_g occupied by the pulse, but because the light makes a round trip, the spread of scattering positions that return at the same moment is half of that. About 2.0 m omits the round-trip factor of 2, and about 1.5 m uses the vacuum speed of light instead of the speed in the fiber, c/n_g. Shorter pulses improve the resolution, but the backscatter from each position becomes weaker, so more averaging is needed for the same temperature precision, a trade-off with measurement time.

optical-sensing-042.question: A strain sensor is built as a Mach–Zehnder interferometer whose one arm is a single-mode fiber of length L = 1.0 m. When axial strain ε is applied to the fiber, the phase change is Δφ = (2πnL/λ) ξ ε (n = 1.46, λ = 1550 nm, and ξ = 0.78 is a factor including the photoelastic effect). Which value is closest to Δφ for ε = 1 µε (1×10⁻⁶)?
choices: About 4.6 rad
About 5.9 rad
About 3.2 rad
optical-sensing-042.explanation: Δφ = 2π × 1.46 × 1.0 m / (1.55×10⁻⁶ m) × 0.78 × 1×10⁻⁶ ≈ 4.6 rad. When the fiber stretches, its length increases and the phase advances, but at the same time the photoelastic effect lowers the index, so the factor ξ ≈ 0.78, which subtracts that part, is applied. About 5.9 rad omits ξ and ignores the index change. About 3.2 rad forgets to multiply by the index n, computing the phase from the length alone instead of the optical path length in the fiber. For the same 1 µε, an FBG's Bragg wavelength shifts by only about 1.2 pm, so an interferometer, which accumulates the change over a long fiber, can measure far smaller strains and vibrations. In exchange, it is equally sensitive to temperature changes.

optical-sensing-043.question: For a uniform FBG with a small index modulation, you want to narrow the reflection band without changing the Bragg wavelength, so that small shifts of the Bragg wavelength are easier to read. Which change to the grating design is correct?
choices: Vary the period gradually along the grating (chirp), because the wavelengths reflected at each position shift and overlap, sharpening the peak
Make the grating longer, since with weak index modulation the bandwidth is nearly inversely proportional to the length
Increase the index modulation, because the larger it is, the better the reflections from each period line up and reinforce, narrowing the band
optical-sensing-043.explanation: In an FBG with a small index modulation, the slight reflections from each period reinforce only when their phases line up over the full grating length. The longer the grating, the stricter it is about phase mismatch, and the reflection bandwidth (the spacing between the first zeros on either side of the main peak) is roughly λB²/(n_eff L), narrowing in inverse proportion to the length L. Varying the period along the grating (chirp) makes each position reflect a slightly different wavelength, so the band broadens instead; chirped gratings are used as broadband reflectors and for dispersion compensation. Increasing the index modulation raises the reflectance, but light is reflected before it reaches deep into the grating, so the effective length shortens and the band broadens. In strong gratings the bandwidth is set by the size of the index modulation.

optical-sensing-044.question: One type of fiber-optic thermometer has a small gallium arsenide (GaAs) crystal at the fiber tip; white light is sent down the fiber, and the temperature is found from the position of the absorption edge in the spectrum of the returning light. Which combination of principle and feature is correct for this method?
choices: As the temperature rises, the band gap widens and the absorption edge moves to shorter wavelengths; its position is found from the total light intensity
As the temperature rises, the crystal's refractive index changes and the reflected intensity increases, so the temperature is found from the change in total returned light
As the temperature rises, the band gap narrows and the absorption edge moves to longer wavelengths; reading the edge wavelength rather than intensity makes it robust to loss
optical-sensing-044.explanation: A semiconductor's band gap narrows as temperature rises, so the absorption edge of GaAs (about 870 nm at room temperature) moves to longer wavelengths with temperature. Reading the wavelength position of the edge in the returned spectrum gives the temperature. Because temperature is converted into a wavelength position rather than an intensity, the reading is hardly affected when fiber bending or connector loss changes the amount of light. The sensing element has no metal or wires and can measure in strong electromagnetic fields, so it is used in transformer windings, microwave heating, and inside MRI equipment. Saying the edge moves to shorter wavelengths reverses the direction. Reading the total light cannot be distinguished from changes in the transmission loss.

optical-sensing-045.question: In Fourier-domain OCT at a wavelength of 1.30 µm, the same position is measured twice with a time interval T = 20 µs, and blood flow speed is found from the phase difference between the two signals (Doppler OCT). If the phase difference Δφ = 4πn v T/λ (v is the velocity component along the beam, and the tissue index is n = 1.35) is 0.50 rad, which value is closest to v?
choices: About 3.8 mm/s
About 1.9 mm/s
About 2.6 mm/s
optical-sensing-045.explanation: v = Δφ λ/(4πnT) = 0.50 × 1.30×10⁻⁶ / (4π × 1.35 × 20×10⁻⁶) ≈ 1.9×10⁻³ m/s, about 1.9 mm/s. When a reflector moves vT along the beam, the light makes a round trip, so the optical path changes by 2nvT and the phase shifts by 4πnvT/λ. About 3.8 mm/s divides by 2π, leaving out the round-trip factor of 2, and about 2.6 mm/s omits the tissue index. The phase wraps beyond ±π, so under these conditions the unambiguous speed is up to about 12 mm/s; for faster flow, T is shortened. Only the component along the beam is measured, so the angle between the vessel and the beam is also needed.
